summary: This work demonstrates a superconducting-qubit quantum simulator of the Bose-Hubbard model on a triangular-ladder lattice with tunable synthetic magnetic flux, preparing and characterizing half-filling ground states through measurements of current-current correlators and bond kinetic energies. The experiments reveal chiral superfluids at $\pi$ flux with staggered loop currents, Meissner superfluids at zero flux with suppressed rung currents, and signatures of bond-ordered insulating phases.
motivation: Frustrated bosonic lattice models with synthetic gauge fields host exotic many-body phases difficult to access classically, and superconducting transmons offer a natural platform for realizing attractive Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians with site-resolved control and rapid repetition rates.
method: An 8-qubit triangular-ladder device with tunable transmon couplers implements rung hopping $J/2\pi = 6.1$ MHz and leg hopping $J_\parallel/2\pi = 2.5$–$20.4$ MHz (or negative). Ground states are prepared via adiabatic ramp at half-filling (4 excitations), and observables are extracted by applying calibrated beamsplitter rotations to map currents and bond kinetic energies onto population imbalances.
result: Chiral current-current correlations $\mathcal{C}$ are orders of magnitude larger at $\pi$ flux ($J_\parallel/J < 0$) than at zero flux, while bond energies alternate in sign at $\pi$ flux but remain uniform at zero flux, yielding a bond-order parameter $O_{\mathrm{BO}}$ peaking near $J_\parallel/J \approx -1$ consistent with theoretical predictions for the chiral superfluid–bond-insulator phase boundary.
